claim: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the project scope.

claim: Wilson and colleagues showed that sensitivity to receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitors can be bypassed by various ligands through reactivation of downstream signaling pathways.
source: In these experiments, Wilson and colleagues show that sensitivity to receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitors can be bypassed by various ligands through reactivation of downstream signaling pathways (Figure 2A; Wilson et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2012, specifically referencing Figure 2A from that publication.

claim: Blocking the receptors for bypassing ligands abrogates their ability to block sensitivity to the original RTK inhibitor.
source: blocking the receptors for these bypassing ligands abrogates their ability to block sensitivity to the original RTK inhibitor (Figure 2C; Wilson et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2012, specifically referencing Figure 2C from that publication.

claim: The effectiveness of therapies targeting specific mutations in receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) is limited by the acquisition of resistance to the drugs over the course of treatment.
source: The effectiveness of therapies targeting specific mutations in receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) is limited by the acquisition of resistance to the drugs over the course of treatment (Mok et al., 2009; Camidge et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mok et al., 2009 and Camidge et al., 2014.

claim: Resistance to RTK inhibitors can be acquired through new mutations that block the action of the RTK inhibitors or their uptake.
source: Resistance can be acquired through new mutations that block the action of the RTK inhibitors or their uptake and/or genetic amplification of downstream target genes of the RTK (Chen and Fu, 2011; Garrett and Arteaga, 2011; Sequist et al., 2011; Gainor and Shaw, 2013; Yang, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Chen and Fu, 2011; Garrett and Arteaga, 2011; Sequist et al., 2011; Gainor and Shaw, 2013; Yang, 2013.

claim: Resistance to RTK inhibitors can be acquired through genetic amplification of downstream target genes of the RTK.
source: Resistance can be acquired through new mutations that block the action of the RTK inhibitors or their uptake and/or genetic amplification of downstream target genes of the RTK (Chen and Fu, 2011; Garrett and Arteaga, 2011; Sequist et al., 2011; Gainor and Shaw, 2013; Yang, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Chen and Fu, 2011; Garrett and Arteaga, 2011; Sequist et al., 2011; Gainor and Shaw, 2013; Yang, 2013.

claim: The engagement of parallel RTK signaling pathways that converge on common downstream survival signals via signals from the tumor microenvironment is a mechanism for acquisition of resistance to RTK inhibitors.
source: Several studies, including this work by Wilson and colleagues, elucidated another mechanism for this acquisition of resistance: the engagement of parallel RTK signaling pathways that converge on common downstream survival signals via signals from the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to multiple studies including Wilson and colleagues' work, indicating citation-based evidence.

claim: Treatment of A204 cells with FGF activated pFRS2 and pERK, inducing resistance to sunitinib.
source: Treatment of A204 (a PDGFR amplified rhabdomyosarcoma cell line) with the ligand FGF activated pFRS2 and pERK, inducing resistance to sunitinib.
evidence: This claim describes experimental results from Wilson et al., 2012, as summarized in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of PD173074 blocked FGF-induced pFRS2 and pERK activation in A204 cells, restoring sensitivity to sunitinib.
source: The addition of a secondary kinase inhibitor, PD173074, blocked FGF-induced pFRS2 and pERK activation, restoring sensitivity to sunitinib.
evidence: This claim describes experimental results from Wilson et al., 2012, as summarized in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of M14 cells with NRG1 activated pHER3 and pAKT, inducing partial resistance to PLX4032.
source: The treatment of M14 (a BRAF-mutated melanoma cell line) with the ligand NRG1 activated pHER3 and pAKT, inducing partial resistance to PLX4032.
evidence: This claim describes experimental results from Wilson et al., 2012, as summarized in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of lapatinib blocked NRG1-induced pHER3 and pAKT activation in M14 cells, restoring sensitivity to PLX4032.
source: The addition of a secondary kinase inhibitor, lapatinib, blocked NRG1-induced pHER3 and pAKT activation, restoring sensitivity to PLX4032.
evidence: This claim describes experimental results from Wilson et al., 2012, as summarized in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of KHM-3S cells with HGF activated pMET and pERK, inducing resistance to Erlotinib.
source: Treatment of KHM-3S (an EGFR-mutated small cell lung cancer cell line) with the ligand HGF activated pMET and pERK, inducing resistance to Erlotinib.
evidence: This claim describes experimental results from Wilson et al., 2012, as summarized in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of crizotinib blocked HGF-induced pMET and pERK activation in KHM-3S cells, restoring sensitivity to erlotinib.
source: The addition of a secondary kinase inhibitor, crizotinib, blocked HGF-induced pMET and pERK activation, restoring sensitivity to erlotinib.
evidence: This claim describes experimental results from Wilson et al., 2012, as summarized in the manuscript.

claim: HGF signaling derived from the tumor microenvironment could bypass EGFR inhibition by activation of MET signaling.
source: Straussman and colleagues demonstrated that HGF signaling derived from the tumor microenvironment could bypass EGFR inhibition by activation of MET signaling (Straussman et al., 2012, also included for replication in the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Straussman et al., 2012.

claim: Multiple growth factor ligands could 'bypass' inhibitor-targeted RTKs.
source: Harbinski and colleagues, in an approach similar to Wilson and colleagues, showed that multiple growth factor ligands could 'bypass' inhibitor-targeted RTKs (Harbinski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harbinski et al., 2012.

claim: FGF ligands could induce resistance to sunitinib in HUVEC cells, which could be reversed by the addition of PD173074.
source: Similar to the experiments with A204 cells above, Welti and colleagues demonstrated that FGF ligands could induce resistance to sunitinib, which could be reversed by the addition of PD173074 (Welti et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Welti et al., 2011.

claim: NRG1 ligand could activate pHER3 and pAKT in 8505C cells in the presence of PLX4032, and this activation could be reversed by the addition of lapatinib.
source: Similar to the experiments on M14 cells above, Montero-Conde and colleagues showed that NRG1 ligand could activate pHER3 and pAKT in the presence of PLX4032, and this activation could be reversed by the addition of lapatinib (Montero-Conde et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Montero-Conde et al., 2013.

claim: HGF ligand can induce resistance to erlotinib in PC-9 and HCC827 cells, and this resistance can be reversed by the addition of crizotinib.
source: Similar to the experiments performed on KHM-S3 cells above, several groups have demonstrated that HGF ligand can induce resistance to erlotinib and that this resistance can be reversed by the addition of crizotinib (Nakagawa et al., 2012; Nakade et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakagawa et al., 2012 and Nakade et al., 2014.

claim: The breast cancer cell line MDA-MB-435 has been shown to be mislabeled and is in fact identical to the M14 melanoma cell line.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rae et al., 2007; Chambers, 2009; and Holliday and Speirs, 2011.
